summary: Discusses implementation decisions for routing in the NSFNET, especially its Backbone. A main concern is limiting routing information so that only the best route, as chosen by a policy decision, gets advertised.

plainLanguage.summary: A big road network has many paths between towns. This explains how the network picks which paths to tell others about, based on rules and not just distance.

questions: how nsfnet chose routes to advertise
how did nsfnet use egp for policy routing
primary secondary routes in routing policy
subtitle: Policy-based routing using EGP between NSFNET backbone and regional networks

tldr.problem: EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) alone cannot enforce routing policies in NSFNET because it lacks the ability to control which networks can advertise routes or to distinguish primary from secondary paths.
tldr.mechanism: Add a rudimentary policy layer on top of EGP: networks select primary and secondary regional representatives through bilateral agreements, metrics encode the preference level, and the backbone validates that only authorized networks advertise routes.
tldr.outcome: This approach let NSFNET backbone manage routing through policy-based agreements while using EGP as the exchange mechanism, protecting networks from unwanted advertisements and creating predictable multi-path routing.

today: RFC 1092 is a historic document describing routing policy architecture used in the NSFNET backbone during the late 1980s. The concepts—policy databases, bilateral agreements, and validation of route advertisements—influenced the later development of BGP and route filtering mechanisms. Though the specific EGP-based system has been superseded by modern routing protocols, the fundamental idea of policy-based routing remains central to internet operations.

sections.title: The Routing Challenge in NSFNET
sections.content:
RFC 1092 discusses implementation decisions for routing in the NSFNET (National Science Foundation Network) backbone, which connected regional networks. The challenge was to ensure packets traveling between regions took reasonable paths while respecting each regional network's preferences.

The RFC focuses on how reachability information is exchanged so the backbone can route packets correctly. The core problem: EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) was chosen as the exchange mechanism, but EGP alone did not provide a way to enforce which networks could advertise which routes or to distinguish between primary and secondary paths.
sections.plainLanguage: NSFNET was like a highway connecting regions. It needed a way for each region to say what networks it serves, but the old routing language did not prevent regions from lying or advertising paths they did not actually have.

sections.title: Policy-Based Routing with EGP
sections.content:
The solution adds policy enforcement on top of EGP. Each network selects specific regional networks as its primary representative to the NSFNET backbone, and optionally designates secondary and tertiary representatives through bilateral agreements with those regional networks and the backbone management.

The primary representative advertises the network with EGP distance zero, while secondary representatives use distance one or higher. If the primary path is available, secondary paths are ignored. If the primary fails, the next-lowest metric path is used.

A Routing Policy Data Base records all bilateral agreements. The backbone periodically compares actual EGP announcements against this database, detecting and reporting any unsolicited representations (a regional network claiming to serve a network it has no agreement to serve).
sections.plainLanguage: Each network picks its main and backup representatives. The main one promises the best path (zero distance), backups promise longer paths. The highway checks the agreement list and complains if someone unauthorized claims to serve a network.

sections.title: Implementation and Autonomous System Numbers
sections.content:
The scheme validates that regional networks use correct autonomous system numbers. The NSFNET backbone itself becomes a separate autonomous system with its own number.

The backbone advertises all routes to regional networks using a fixed EGP metric of 128, which encourages traffic to prefer backdoor routes (direct connections between regions) if available and desired, rather than forcing all traffic through the backbone.

Regional networks are expected to handle bilateral agreements with their leaf networks, configure EGP metrics from policy data, and provide the backbone with any necessary metrics data.
sections.plainLanguage: Each region gets its own identifier number. The backbone tells everyone 'the cost through me is 128' so regions can decide if a direct path is better. Everyone tells the backbone about their agreements ahead of time.

sections.title: Addressing EGP Limitations
sections.content:
This policy layer solves several EGP problems: it allows networks to prevent unauthorized representation, supports primary and secondary paths (which plain EGP metrics do not clearly express), prevents false advertisements (a regional network claiming zero distance to a network it does not actually serve), and ensures routes through the backbone can be deprioritized in favor of backdoor routes when desired.

The approach preserves EGP as the actual exchange protocol while layering policy on top, avoiding the need to redesign routing protocols entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: The old language did not have a clear way to say 'main path vs backup' or 'this person is lying.' This adds that on top, using the old language for talking but agreements for truth.
